title: A-V-L

segments.voice: Yesterday, S-M-Ch: simcha, joy with a guest list. Your line was joy. Who did you share it with? Today, the root for the other side of a life, and the people who sit beside it. Day one thousand four hundred four.

Three friends hear that a man named Job has lost everything: his animals, his servants, his children, and now his health. They each set out from home and meet up to go to him together. From a distance they hardly recognize him. They weep, they tear their robes, they throw dust in the air. And then they do the thing the book remembers. They sit down with him on the ground, for seven days and seven nights, and nobody says a word. Later, they'll talk, and the talking won't go well. But the first week, they got exactly right.
screen: `THREE FRIENDS SET OUT.` → `THEY SIT ON THE GROUND.` → `SEVEN DAYS. NOT A WORD.`

segments.voice: A-V-L. Alef, vet, lamed. Avel: a mourner. Avelut: the time of mourning. Turn it a few ways. First, a father in Genesis. Jacob's sons bring him their brother Joseph's coat, torn and bloodied, and he believes Joseph is dead. His children come to comfort him, and he won't be comforted. "For I will go down into the grave unto my son mourning." Mourning, there, is avel. Not a passing sadness. A state you live in. Second, Job's friends. The text says why they kept silent: "for they saw that his grief was very great." The rabbis turned that silence into a custom. Visitors to a house of mourning wait for the mourner to speak first. You don't arrive with a speech. You arrive. Third, the shape of the time. The first week after a burial is called shiva, from the word for seven. The mourners stay home, often sitting low, and the community comes to them, bringing food and filling the room so that the prayers can be said there. Then the mourning loosens in stages, over the following weeks and the year. Grief isn't told to be over by a date. It's given rooms to move through. Fourth, the comforters' words. When visitors leave a house of mourning, the traditional line asks that God comfort the mourner among the mourners of Zion and Jerusalem. Even the comfort puts the mourner inside a larger group. An avel is someone the community is holding up.
screen: `JACOB: I WILL GO DOWN MOURNING.` · `JOB'S FRIENDS: SILENCE FIRST.` · `SHIVA: THE COMMUNITY COMES TO YOU.` · `AMONG THE MOURNERS OF ZION.` · then, large: `YOU DON'T SPEAK. YOU ARRIVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with someone mourning. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who is grieving. A friend, a neighbor, a coworker, someone in your own family. It might be recent. It might be years ago and still there. You don't have to fix it, and you don't have to find words. Just sit with them in your mind, the way Job's friends sat on the ground. Let the silence be the company. If you are the one mourning, let yourself be sat with. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
screen: `BRING SOMEONE TO MIND.` · `NO WORDS NEEDED.` · `JUST SIT.`

segments.voice: A-V-L. Alef, vet, lamed: the root of avel, a mourner, and avelut, the time of mourning. Today's word.
Your line: mourning. Today, reach one person who's grieving. A short message, a meal, a visit. Let them speak first, and listen. Day one thousand four hundred four.

howItsDone: Jewish mourners sit shiva, staying home after the burial while the community visits, brings food and makes up a prayer quorum; by custom visitors wait for the mourner to speak first, and on leaving they offer the traditional words of comfort.

notes: Job 2:11–13 paraphrased (three friends, weeping, tearing robes, dust, sitting on the ground seven days and seven nights in silence); 2:13's last clause quoted from KJV. Confirm.
Genesis 37:35 quoted from KJV; the word for mourning is avel. No claim is made about which verse first uses the root (Genesis 27:41 already has yemei evel).
Custom that comforters may not speak until the mourner speaks: Moed Katan 28b, derived from Job 2:13. Paraphrased; confirm.
Shiva customs (staying home, sitting low, meals, minyan in the house) and staged mourning (shloshim, the year) described without numbers beyond 'seven'; confirm phrasing.
Traditional comforters' formula (HaMakom yenachem etchem betoch she'ar avelei Tzion viYerushalayim) paraphrased, not quoted.
